help.title: Tolerance Interval Capability
help.body:
Description
Tolerance Interval Capability answers the question: "Given n measurements, what mean-to-limit margin do I need so that at least p × 100 % of the population clears the spec limit, with (1−α) × 100 % confidence?"

What is the k-factor?
The k-factor is a sample-size-aware safety multiplier. It tells you how many standard deviations your process mean must sit away from the limit per unit of standard deviation, given the uncertainty introduced by having only n measurements.

Think of it this way: if you had infinitely many measurements you would know the true population mean and standard deviation exactly, and you would only need a z-score (e.g. z = 3.09 for p = 0.999). But with a finite sample your estimates of mean and SD carry sampling error, so the required margin must be wider to maintain the stated confidence. The k-factor grows as n decreases — for n = 10 and p = 0.999 at 95 % confidence, k ≈ 5.20, compared to k → 3.09 as n → ∞.

Mathematically, k comes from the non-central t-distribution:
k(n, p, γ) = tν, δ, γ / √n
where ν = n − 1 (degrees of freedom), δ = √n · Φ⁻¹(p) (non-centrality parameter), γ = confidence level (e.g. 0.95).

Outputs
Capability Needed — the required ratio (x̄ − L) / (k · s) must equal 1.0 (i.e. the tolerance limit exactly touches the spec). In practice your process must achieve C ≥ 1.0. The required mean given an expected SD is also shown.

Capability Calculated — if you supply observed x̄ and s (or select a variable):
C = (x̄ − L) / (k · s) [lower limit case]
C = (L − x̄) / (k · s) [upper limit case]
PASS if C ≥ 1.0, FAIL if C < 1.0. The achieved tolerance limit TL = x̄ ∓ k · s is also reported.

Capability Chart — when observed x̄ and s are supplied, a bell curve centred at x̄ is drawn with the spec limit L shown as a vertical red line. The tail on the failing side of L is shaded:
  █ Blue shading — PASS: the tail beyond L is small; the process clears the spec.
  █ Orange shading — FAIL: the tail beyond L is large; the process does not meet the requirement.
  No shading — the process is so far from the spec limit that essentially zero of the distribution falls beyond L (e.g. mean = 50, s = 2, L = 15). The tail is too small to appear on the chart. This is a highly capable process and is still a PASS.
A dashed blue vertical line marks the observed mean x̄; a dotted green line marks the achieved tolerance limit TL. The annotation box inside the chart shows k, TL, C, and the PASS / FAIL verdict.

Inputs
n — total number of individual measurements (integer ≥ 2). When a dataset variable is selected, n is computed automatically from the non-missing observations and the Sample size spinner value is ignored.
Confidence — statistical confidence in the tolerance statement (default 0.95).
Reliability — the minimum fraction of the population that must clear the limit (default 0.999).
Limit value L — the one-sided specification (e.g. minimum pull force, maximum temperature).
Observed x̄ and s — optional; supply these (or select a dataset variable) to see whether your current process passes. When a variable is selected, the sample mean and standard deviation are computed from the data and the sample size n is taken from the variable (missing values are excluded).

Note
This procedure assumes the characteristic is normally distributed. It is equivalent to a one-sided normal tolerance interval as described in ASTM E2810, ISO 16269-6, and Minitab's Tolerance Intervals (Normal) procedure.
